transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE, optional), Martin Yu (HelixAI ML Infra), Sara Olsen (HelixAI CTO), Diego Ramos (HelixAI SRE), Nina Patel (HelixAI Data Scientist)

[00:00] Alex Kim: okay hey everyone thanks for coming, we'll jump straight into the deep dive; objective for today is to go over architecture tuning around Llama/Mistral/Qwen fam, focus on MoE routing overhead and RoPE scaling — and align on benchmarks you'd like us to run
[00:18] Martin Yu: yep thanks Alex, we mainly care about p50/p95/p99 latency at our 200 qps realistic mix and tail behavior when context jumps to 16k, also cost impact since we are evaluating dedicated vs hosted, also we have on-prem regulatory constraints for some logs
[00:34] Priya Rao: got it — so we'll cover KV cache sizing, continuous batching, quantization profiles, and MoE routing mostly. quick high level: MoE models give compute efficiency for FLOPS per token but routing adds memory and all-to-all cost at layer boundaries, especially in small batch/low concurrency setups
[01:02] Sara Olsen: can you expand on the routing all-to-all? that's a big concern for us, our infra doesn't like bursty all-to-all patterns
[01:12] Priya Rao: sure — at a high level the gate picks top-k experts per token; that selection implies movement of tokens to experts, which in distributed setups becomes an all-to-all communication; on H100/A100 this shows up as increased collective latency and temporary memory amplification because each GPU holds extra buffers for incoming tokens
[01:35] Diego Ramos: are there tricks to reduce that? like expert locality or padding?
[01:41] Priya Rao: yes — we discussed two main levers: 1) expert placement co-located with padded micro-batches for affinity, 2) routing constraints like limiting top-k to 1 (top-1) for some layers to reduce shuffling. both reduce FLOPS benefits slightly but cut all-to-all overhead. Also asynchronous routing with overlap of compute/comm helps — but it complicates kernel scheduling
[02:10] Jordan Lee: also there's a batch-size sweet spot. In continuous batching runtime we can merge requests into bigger micro-batches to amortize routing cost; but that increases tail latency. For HelixAI's 200 qps target, we can tune batching windows to trade latency vs throughput
[02:31] Martin Yu: ok interesting — what about KV cache? When we go to 16k context the KV cache grows a lot; do you shard KV across GPUs or keep local copies? memory will be the limiter
[02:44] Priya Rao: we shard KV across GPUs and keep a compact representation where possible; but note RoPE scaling interacts here — rotary embeddings are computed per token and included in KV keys so if you double context you double KV footprint. We use chunked KV eviction and prefix caching in the runtime: hot prefixes kept in fast local memory, older history evicted or stored in lower tier (SSD) for cold retrieval. For on-prem that SSD tier configuration matters operationally
[03:15] Nina Patel: side question on RoPE — we've seen hallucination drift at longer contexts in some models. Is that a RoPE effect or something in training?
[03:25] Priya Rao: good question — RoPE scaling mismatch can cause phase drift; some variants of RoPE need adjusted scaling law for extrapolation beyond native sequence length. For Mistral and some Llama forks we see better long-context stability when using scaled RoPE or ALiBi-like linear bias hybrids. But you often need small finetune or prefix-tuning to stabilize behavior beyond training lengths
[03:52] Sara Olsen: any concrete numbers you can share, like p99 delta with MoE vs dense?
[03:59] Priya Rao: rough numbers from earlier benchmarks: dense 70B on 8xH100 baseline p99 around ~450-600ms for 1k prompt (depends on token length), MoE equivalent sometimes shows 20-30% lower compute cost per token but p99 can worsen by 1.5-2x if routing isn't optimized in the cluster due to all-to-all stalls. With routing optimizations (top-1, locality) we recover most of the p99 and keep the cost win ~10-15%
[04:27] Diego Ramos: hmm okay, and quantization? can that help reduce KV memory?
[04:34] Priya Rao: yes, quantization helps different parts: weights can be q4/q8 which reduces model footprint and memory bandwidth; activations including KV often use int8 or BF16 paths. But quantizing KV itself has tradeoffs — aggressive quantization increases generation noise. For earlier models we've used q4_k and q4_0 variants; q4_k sometimes gives better MLP activation fidelity at the cost of slightly higher memory than q4_0. We plan to include q8 and int8 runs in the benchmark to show delta on both latency and quality
[05:05] Martin Yu: any tooling for quality regression checks? we can't sacrifice hallucination rates for cost
[05:11] Alex Kim: yes — Redwood Optimize ties quality monitors to prompt sets; we'll run eval harness comparing rouge/qa accuracy and a small set of custom tests you provide. Priya will include quality metrics in the benchmark report
[05:25] [crosstalk] Nina Patel: that would be great, we'll prepare a 200-prompt seed set with edge cases
[05:33] Priya Rao: perfect. On the runtime side another caveat: RoPE and position embedding implementation needs to match model's training variant. For Qwen we sometimes see different RoPE parameterization — if that's mismatched you get subtle token-level logits misalignments and KV mismatches at retrieval time
[05:52] Sara Olsen: can Redwood auto-detect RoPE variant?
[05:55] Priya Rao: runtime will try heuristics but for production we request model metadata and ideally a small verification run. We'll include a small test harness that checks token-level logits on a reference prompt to confirm RoPE compatibility
[06:12] Martin Yu: about VPC/on-prem — we'd want private control plane and no egress. How do you handle key management and audit logs?
[06:21] Alex Kim: for Private deployments we support customer KMS integrations (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, HSMs) and audit logs shipped to customer-controlled buckets. There's also an on-prem bundle with no external egress and local console option. We'll send SOC2/ISO docs as requested
[06:36] Diego Ramos: network-wise, what bandwidth should we plan for MoE all-to-all?
[06:41] Priya Rao: depends on expert count and tokens per step; as a rule of thumb plan for additional transient network load equal to ~20-40% of nominal activation traffic per token for 8-32 experts in a typical setup. If you have constrained network, it's better to restrict routing or favor local experts to limit peaks
[07:02] Jordan Lee: also kernel selection matters — on H100 we use fused attention + rotary ops that reduce memory passes; on A100 some kernels are less fused which increases bytes moved. We'll include per-hardware kernel mapping in the report
[07:20] Martin Yu: can you run benchmarks on both H100 and A100? HelixAI has a mixed fleet for now
[07:25] Priya Rao: yes, we can run both. For the pilot we'd recommend H100 baseline and A100 comparison; call out kernel differences and quantization deltas
[07:36] [00:07:48] Alex Kim: let's sketch the benchmark plan: 1) baseline dense model (e.g., Llama-70B) 2) MoE variant with top-1 vs top-2 routing experiments 3) RoPE scaled vs default for 16k context 4) quantization profiles q4_0, q4_k, int8 5) continuous batching variations for 200 qps traffic
[08:02] Martin Yu: timeline?
[08:04] Alex Kim: we can deliver initial CSV and summary in ~7 business days for H100 runs; with A100 add 2-3 days. So target wrapped artifacts by 2026-12-10 for the H100 set
[08:14] Nina Patel: please include per-token cost estimate, not just total GPU hours
[08:18] Alex Kim: will do; cost per M token and per-response will be in the pricing + benchmark spreadsheet
[08:24] Diego Ramos: one more ops question: if we do dedicated capacity with pinned experts, can we reduce routing overhead?
[08:31] Priya Rao: yes, dedicated pools allow us to control placement and reduce cross-tenant noise, and with reserved capacity we can pin experts onto a set of GPUs to remove unnecessary all-to-all across the whole cluster. That's one of the big wins for Dedicated for MoE workloads
[08:49] Sara Olsen: what about fallback strategies? if an expert is OOM or slow how do you keep tail from exploding?
[08:56] Priya Rao: we have fallback policies: reroute to dense shard of the model, fall back to smaller dense model, or synthetic fill with cached completions for specific prefixes. The platform supports canary routing and automatic fallback when p99 goes beyond threshold
[09:13] Martin Yu: cool. Anything else we should prep from HelixAI side?
[09:18] Martin Yu: we'll provide the prompt set, sample logs, and target p99. Also we may want a short on-prem smoke test for the Private bundle during pilot
[09:28] Alex Kim: great. last part — replicate a quick readout of next steps
[09:33] Alex Kim: Redwood: run MoE + RoPE benchmarks (Priya), include quant profiles and quality checks, share security docs and Dedicated pricing (Alex). HelixAI: share prompt set and p99 targets, confirm VPC peering window (Diego).
[09:48] Sara Olsen: sounds good, thanks.
[09:51] Alex Kim: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifact links and schedule the pilot kickoff once benchmarks look good.
[09:58] [end of recording]
